subject: Cloud Computing
title: IAM: The Gatekeeper
description: A tiny lesson with a big payoff: IAM: The Gatekeeper.

hook.text: Every cloud action — launching a server, reading a file, deleting a database — goes through IAM first.

buildup.text: Identity and Access Management controls who can do what. Users, roles, and policies define permissions.

discovery.text: An IAM policy is a JSON document that says: this identity can perform these actions on these resources.

twist.text: IAM policies are powerful but complex. A single misconfigured policy can expose an entire cloud account.

climax.text: IAM is arguably the most important cloud service. Get it wrong and nothing else matters.

punchline.text: IAM is the front door to your cloud. Lock it properly.

quiz.question: What role does IAM play in cloud security?
options: It controls who can perform what actions on which cloud resources
It encrypts all data stored in the cloud automatically
It monitors network traffic for suspicious activity

details.summary: Identity and Access Management controls who can access cloud resources and what they can do. IAM policies define permissions for users, groups, and service accounts, making it the single most critical security control in any cloud environment.
details.whyItMatters: Misconfigured IAM is the leading cause of cloud security incidents. Getting identity right is the foundation every other security control depends on.
takeaways: IAM controls authentication and authorization in the cloud
Policies define who can access which resources and how
Misconfigured IAM is the top cause of cloud breaches

faq.question: What is the difference between authentication and authorization?
faq.answer: Authentication verifies who you are, typically through passwords, tokens, or certificates. Authorization determines what you are allowed to do once authenticated. IAM manages both, ensuring only verified identities perform only permitted actions.

faq.question: How should IAM policies be structured?
faq.answer: Follow the principle of least privilege: grant only the minimum permissions needed for each role. Use groups rather than individual user policies, regularly audit permissions, and remove unused accounts and roles promptly.
